title: The Dot Product
lead: The dot product multiplies two vectors to give a scalar. This section computes it from components and from the angle between the vectors, uses it to test orthogonality and find direction angles, projects one vector onto another, and calculates the work a constant force does.
objectives: Calculate the dot product of two given vectors.
Determine whether two given vectors are perpendicular.
Find the direction cosines of a given vector.
Explain what is meant by the vector projection of one vector onto another vector, and describe how to compute it.
Calculate the work done by a given force.
summary_html:
• The dot product, or scalar product, of two vectors $\kvecu=\langle u_{1},u_{2},u_{3}\rangle$ and $\kvecv=\langle v_{1},v_{2},v_{3}\rangle$ is $\kvecu\cdot \kvecv=u_{1}v_{1}+u_{2}v_{2}+u_{3}v_{3}.$
  • The dot product satisfies the following properties:
  • $\kvecu\cdot \kvecv=\kvecv\cdot \kvecu $
  • $\kvecu\cdot (\kvecv+\kvecw)=\kvecu\cdot \kvecv+\kvecu\cdot \kvecw $
  • $c(\kvecu\cdot \kvecv)=(c\kvecu)\cdot \kvecv=\kvecu\cdot (c\kvecv)$
  • $\kvecv\cdot \kvecv={\| \kvecv\|}^{2}$
  • The dot product of two vectors can be expressed, alternatively, as $\kvecu\cdot \kvecv=\| \kvecu\| \| \kvecv\| \cos \ktheta .$ This form of the dot product is useful for finding the measure of the angle formed by two vectors.
  • Vectors $\kvecu $ and $\kvecv $ are orthogonal if $\kvecu\cdot \kvecv=0.$
  • The angles formed by a nonzero vector and the coordinate axes are called the direction angles for the vector. The cosines of these angles are known as the direction cosines.
  • The vector projection of $\kvecv $ onto $\kvecu $ is the vector ${\text{proj}}_{\kvecu}\kvecv=\frac{\kvecu\cdot \kvecv}{{\| \kvecu\|}^{2}}\kvecu.$ The magnitude of this vector is known as the scalar projection of $\kvecv $ onto $\kvecu $, given by ${\text{comp}}_{\kvecu}\kvecv=\frac{\kvecu\cdot \kvecv}{\| \kvecu\|}.$
  • Work is done when a force is applied to an object, causing displacement. When the force is represented by the vector $\kvecF$ and the displacement is represented by the vector $\kvecs$, then the work done W is given by the formula $W=\kvecF\cdot s=\| \kvecF\| \| \kvecs\| \cos \ktheta .$

exercises.prompt: Use vectors to show that a parallelogram with equal diagonals is a rectangle.

answer.solution: Let the parallelogram have sides $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ from one vertex; its diagonals are $\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}$ and $\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{v}.$ By the properties of the dot product, $\|\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}\|^{2}=(\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v})\cdot(\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v})=\|\mathbf{u}\|^{2}+2\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}+\|\mathbf{v}\|^{2}$ and $\|\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{v}\|^{2}=\|\mathbf{u}\|^{2}-2\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}+\|\mathbf{v}\|^{2}.$ If the diagonals are equal, subtracting gives $4\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}=0,$ so $\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}=0:$ the adjacent sides are orthogonal, every angle of the parallelogram is a right angle, and it is a rectangle.

exercises.prompt: Use vectors to show that the diagonals of a rhombus are perpendicular.

answer.solution: Let the rhombus have sides $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ from one vertex, with $\|\mathbf{u}\|=\|\mathbf{v}\|$ since its sides are equal. Its diagonals are $\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}$ and $\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{v},$ and $(\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v})\cdot(\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{v})=\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{v}=\|\mathbf{u}\|^{2}-\|\mathbf{v}\|^{2}=0.$ Two nonzero vectors with dot product zero are orthogonal, so the diagonals are perpendicular.

exercises.prompt: Show that $\textbf{u}\cdot (\textbf{v}+\textbf{w})=\textbf{u}\cdot \textbf{v}+\textbf{u}\cdot \textbf{w}$ is true for any vectors $\text{u}$, $\text{v}$, and $\text{w}$.

answer.solution: Let $\mathbf{u}=\langle u_{1},u_{2},u_{3}\rangle,$ $\mathbf{v}=\langle v_{1},v_{2},v_{3}\rangle$ and $\mathbf{w}=\langle w_{1},w_{2},w_{3}\rangle.$ Then $\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{w}=\langle v_{1}+w_{1},v_{2}+w_{2},v_{3}+w_{3}\rangle$ and, by the distributive property of real numbers, $\mathbf{u}\cdot(\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{w})=u_{1}(v_{1}+w_{1})+u_{2}(v_{2}+w_{2})+u_{3}(v_{3}+w_{3})=(u_{1}v_{1}+u_{2}v_{2}+u_{3}v_{3})+(u_{1}w_{1}+u_{2}w_{2}+u_{3}w_{3})=\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{w}.$

exercises.prompt: Consider $\textbf{u}=\langle a,b,c\rangle$ a nonzero three-dimensional vector. Let $\cos \alpha ,$ $\cos β,$ and $\cos γ$ be the direction cosines of $\text{u}$. Show that ${\cos }^{2}\alpha +{\cos }^{2}β+{\cos }^{2}γ=1.$

answer.solution: The direction cosines of $\mathbf{u}=\langle a,b,c\rangle$ are $\cos\alpha=\frac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{i}}{\|\mathbf{u}\|}=\frac{a}{\|\mathbf{u}\|},$ $\cos\beta=\frac{b}{\|\mathbf{u}\|}$ and $\cos\gamma=\frac{c}{\|\mathbf{u}\|}.$ So $\cos^{2}\alpha+\cos^{2}\beta+\cos^{2}\gamma=\frac{a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}}{\|\mathbf{u}\|^{2}}=\frac{a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}}{a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}}=1.$

For the following exercises, determine whether the statement is true or false. Justify the answer with a proof or a counterexample.

For vectors $\textbf{a}$ and $\textbf{b}$ and any given scalar $c,$ $c(\textbf{a}\cdot \textbf{b})=(c\textbf{a})\cdot \textbf{b}.$

For the following exercises, determine whether the statement is true or false. Justify the answer with a proof or a counterexample.

If $\textbf{a}\cdot \textbf{b}=0,$ then $\textbf{a}$ is perpendicular to $\textbf{b}.$

answer.solution: True for nonzero vectors: by the theorem on orthogonal vectors, nonzero vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ with $\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=0$ meet at a right angle, since $\|\mathbf{a}\|\|\mathbf{b}\|\cos\theta=0$ forces $\cos\theta=0.$ If either vector is the zero vector, $\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=0$ always, and the zero vector has no direction of its own, so the statement needs $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ to be nonzero.

The projection has the direction of $\kvecu$, and the opposite direction when $\ktheta$ is obtuse.

then.why: A vector is its length times the unit vector in its direction; the sign is $+$ for an acute $\ktheta$ and $-$ for an obtuse one.

steps.cap: $\kvecu\cdot\kvecv$ has the sign of $\cos\ktheta$, positive for an acute angle and negative for an obtuse one, so it carries the sign itself.
